ket-bra-bridge.idea: Two lists of numbers can tell us how likely a quantum test is to give a particular result.
ket-bra-bridge.explanation: Write the amplitudes of a state in a column. This is its ket. For the outcome you want to test, turn its normalized column into a row and change i to −i. This row is its bra. Multiply matching entries of the bra and the prepared ket, then add. Square the size of the sum to get the chance of that outcome.

example.title: Testing the first basis state
steps: The ket (3,4i)/5 has bra (3,−4i)/5. Its norm squared is one.
Its overlap with (1,0) is 3/5, so that outcome’s chance is 9/25.

terms.definition: The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

state-coordinates.idea: Changing the order of a list does not change what the list describes if the labels move with it.
state-coordinates.explanation: A basis is a set of reference states. Each number in the list belongs to one reference. For example, if the first number goes with “up”, it must still go with “up” when the list is reordered.

example.title: Reordering three labels
steps: In order (e₁,e₂,e₃), the amplitudes are (1,i,2)/√6.
In order (e₃,e₁,e₂), they become (2,1,i)/√6. The chance for e₃ stays 2/3.

terms.definition: Three normalized, mutually orthogonal reference states.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

outer-product-action.idea: One quantum rule can test how much of an input matches one state and turn that amount into another state.
outer-product-action.explanation: First compare the input wave with a chosen reference wave. Their overlap is a number with size and timing. Use that number to multiply a second reference wave. This rule is called an outer product. Its output is a wave, ready for the next calculation.

example.title: A map into the first direction
steps: Take u = (1,0) and v = (1,i)/√2. The map |u⟩⟨v| acts on w = (0,1).
The overlap is −i/√2, so the output is (−i/√2,0).

terms.definition: The two reference vectors defining the map.
The input vector.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

unitary-basis-change.idea: The same state can be written using different sets of reference directions.
unitary-basis-change.explanation: Imagine rotating the grid on a map. The coordinates change even though the place stays put. In a quantum calculation, change both the numbers for the state and the rule for reading the meter. A unitary change keeps wave lengths and overlaps the same.

example.title: The same energy in a new basis
steps: An energy matrix diag(2,6) eV becomes [[4,−2],[−2,4]] eV in the plus/minus basis.
The original first state becomes (1,1)/√2. Using both new descriptions still gives mean energy 2 eV.

terms.definition: Matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors in old coordinates.
Conjugate transpose: swap rows and columns, then reverse imaginary signs.
The same observable’s matrices in the old and new coordinates.
A matrix with diagonal entries 2 and 6 and zero elsewhere.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.
A reversible change that preserves state lengths and overlaps, so the total probability stays one.

adjoints-and-observables.idea: A table that represents a measurable quantity must pass a simple matching test in this finite model.
adjoints-and-observables.explanation: Reflect the entries across the diagonal from top left to bottom right. Change i to −i in each entry. If the resulting table matches the original, the matrix is called Hermitian. This ensures that its possible readings are real numbers.

example.title: Checking one energy matrix
steps: Take E₀[[1,2i],[−2i,3]]. Swap rows and columns, then change i to −i.
The original matrix returns, so it is Hermitian and its energy eigenvalues are real.

terms.definition: The matrix being checked.
The adjoint, made by conjugating and transposing.
A chosen positive energy unit.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.
For a matrix, swapping its rows and columns and taking the complex conjugate of each entry gives the original matrix. Taking a conjugate changes i to −i.

spectral-projectors.idea: A measurement rule can be built from its possible readings.
spectral-projectors.explanation: Imagine a separate filter for each reading. The filter, called a projector, keeps the part of the state that would give that reading. Multiply each kept part by its reading and add the results. Different states with the same reading go through the same filter.

example.title: Two energy outcomes
steps: For E₀[[3,1],[1,3]], the plus state has energy 4E₀ and the minus state has energy 2E₀.
A first-basis input has chance 1/2 for each, so its mean is 3E₀.

terms.definition: One distinct measurement value.
Projector onto all states with that value.
Add the listed terms.
A positive reference energy.

degeneracy-and-compatible-set.idea: A single meter reading can fit more than one quantum state.
degeneracy-and-compatible-set.explanation: For example, two different wave patterns could have the same energy. This sharing is called degeneracy. A second measurement can sometimes tell the states apart while preserving their first reading. Such a pair of measurements is called compatible.

example.title: An unresolved energy pair
steps: States e₁ and e₂ both have energy E₀. Prepare 0.6e₁ + 0.8e₂.
Energy is certainly E₀, while a compatible test distinguishing e₁ from e₂ gives chances 0.36 and 0.64.

terms.definition: More than one independent state sharing a measurement value.
Two orthogonal normalized reference states.
Their shared energy.
The measurements can have joint definite-outcome states.

operator-functions.idea: Sometimes a new measurement rule simply changes the number assigned to each possible result.
operator-functions.explanation: Imagine a meter that displays the square of its old reading. A state with a definite reading of 3 now has a definite reading of 9. A function of a measurement operator applies that number rule to its allowed values while keeping the same reference states.

example.title: Evolving two energies
steps: For energies 0 and 2E₀, choose time so E₀t/ℏ = π/4.
The two time multipliers are 1 and −i. An equal input becomes (1,−i)/√2.

operator-functions.equation: time multiplier for energy E = exp(−iEt/ℏ)

terms.definition: The energy of that component.
The reference energy in the example.
Elapsed time.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A unit-size phase factor with angle −α.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A mathematical rule that acts on a state or function to give another state or function.

projector-probability.idea: A projection keeps only the part of a state that matches a chosen outcome.
projector-probability.explanation: Start with a state whose outcome chances add to one. Square the length of the kept part to get the chance of this outcome. If it happens, divide the kept part by its own length to describe the new state. A part with zero length means the outcome cannot occur.

example.title: Keeping two coordinates
steps: Project (1,2i,2)/3 onto its first two coordinates. The kept weight is (1 + 4)/9 = 5/9.
If that outcome occurs, the normalized state is (1,2i,0)/√5.

terms.definition: The selected outcome’s projector.
The normalized input state.
Vector length.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

degenerate-luders.idea: A measurement can give one result for several distinct states.
degenerate-luders.explanation: Suppose the meter shows the same reading for two possible states. An ideal measurement that only checks that reading keeps their whole combination, including how their waves line up. A more precise meter can tell them apart and change that combination. Erasing its extra reading afterward does not undo the change.

example.title: Keeping the zero-energy subspace
steps: Prepare (e₁ + e₂ + e₃)/√3, with the first two states sharing zero energy.
Recording zero energy ideally leaves (e₁ + e₂)/√2, including its relative phase.

terms.definition: An ideal measurement update that keeps the whole part belonging to the recorded value.
Three orthogonal normalized reference states.
The relative-phase information between parts of a state.

sequential-filters.idea: After a quantum filter gives a result, use the resulting state to predict the next test.
sequential-filters.explanation: Suppose you keep only trials that pass the first filter. Those kept trials are the input for filter two. In a written product AB, B acts first and A acts second. Reversing them can change the chances.

example.title: Two successful filters
steps: Start in |0⟩. A plus filter succeeds with chance 1/2.
For that selected plus state, a subsequent |1⟩ filter succeeds with chance 1/2. Both succeed with chance 1/4.

sequential-filters.equation: joint probability = first probability × conditional second probability

complete-projective-measurement.idea: Measuring a system and throwing away the reading can still affect its next measurement.
complete-projective-measurement.explanation: Each possible reading leaves its own state. If the reading was lost, work out what each of these states would predict and average with the chances of the first readings. Treating the original wave as untouched can give the wrong answer.

example.title: An ignored basis measurement
steps: Prepare |+⟩ and measure the 0/1 basis, then discard the result.
The two branches are equally likely. A later plus test has chance 1/2, rather than the original certainty.

complete-projective-measurement.equation: later probability = sum of (branch weight × branch probability)

terms.definition: The normalized equal sum of |0⟩ and |1⟩.

commutator-products.idea: When order matters, keep track of which of two rules acted first.
commutator-products.explanation: The commutator measures the difference between applying B then A and applying A then B. With a product of rules, more than one change of order may contribute to that difference. Keep each term in its original order when doing the algebra.

example.title: A cancellation check
steps: Let X swap coordinates and Z reverse the second coordinate’s sign. Since X² is the identity, [Z,X²] = 0.
The two expansion terms are opposite diagonal matrices, so they cancel.

terms.definition: The commutator AB − BA.
Operators whose products are defined on the input.
The difference between applying two rules in one order and in the opposite order. Zero means the orders give the same result on the states being considered.

covariance-uncertainty.idea: Two readings can each have a spread and also tend to vary together.
covariance-uncertainty.explanation: First subtract the average from each reading to measure its deviation. In a quantum calculation, multiplying the two deviation rules in opposite orders can give different answers. Average the two orders to get the covariance used here. It can strengthen the lower limit on the spreads.

example.title: Two matrices and one state
steps: Let X swap two coordinates and Z reverse the second sign. For state (√3/2,1/2), their variances are 1/4 and 3/4.
The product is 3/16, equal to the covariance squared. Here the extra order-difference contribution is zero.

terms.definition: The average squared deviation from the mean.
Here, the average of the two possible orders of the deviation product.

translation-generator.idea: Sliding a whole wave pattern to the right moves each old feature the same distance.
translation-generator.explanation: Suppose a peak was at position 2 and is shifted right by 3. At position 5 we should now use the old value at 2. That is why a rightward shift by a uses the old function at x − a. The coordinate grid stays put.

example.title: Moving a Gaussian
steps: A Gaussian is centred at −1 nm. Translate it by +3 nm.
Its new centre is +2 nm, with the same width and total probability.

terms.definition: Position coordinate.
The translation distance.
Position amplitudes before and after translation.

parity-operator.idea: Reflecting a state is different from measuring its reflection symmetry.
parity-operator.explanation: Reflection replaces x by −x. An even part stays the same and an odd part changes sign; applying this operation does not choose one of those measurement outcomes.

example.title: Reflecting a mixed-parity pure state
steps: Prepare (√3/2)u + (1/2)v, with even u and odd v.
Reflection gives (√3/2)u − (1/2)v, retaining both parts.

terms.definition: The parity or reflection operator.
Normalized even and odd reference states.
The position amplitude.
Position relative to the reflection center.

spectral-time-evolution.idea: When the energy rule stays fixed, each energy part of a wave advances at its own steady rate.
spectral-time-evolution.explanation: Separate the state into its definite-energy parts. The timing, or phase, of each part changes at a rate set by its energy. Put the parts back together before predicting a position or spin measurement. Their shares in an energy measurement stay fixed.

example.title: A quarter-turn phase
steps: Use energy frequencies 0 and 3 radians per second, starting with equal amplitudes. After π/6 seconds the second phase factor is −i.
The state is (1,−i)/√2. Its energy chances remain 1/2 each.

terms.definition: That component’s energy.
Elapsed time.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

heisenberg-picture.idea: Two different bookkeeping choices give the same prediction for a changing quantum system.
heisenberg-picture.explanation: In one choice the state changes with time and the meter rule stays fixed. In the other, called the Heisenberg picture, keep the starting state and change the meter rule. Both describe what the same physical meter will read.

example.title: Two descriptions of one two-state experiment
steps: Start with equal amplitudes (1,1)/√2. The second energy component gains phase −π/3, and X swaps the two coordinates.
Using the changed state gives mean X = cos(π/3) = 1/2. Keeping the state fixed and transforming X gives the same 1/2.

terms.definition: The time-evolution operator.
Observable in the evolving-state description.
Observable in the fixed-state description.
The two-state observable that swaps the reference coordinates.
Conjugate transpose: swap rows and columns, then reverse imaginary signs.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

ordered-time-steps.idea: Switching the order of two short pushes can change the final state.
ordered-time-steps.explanation: In a written product, the rightmost rule acts first. Put the first pulse there and the later one to its left. If reversing the pulses gives a different result, say that the rules do not commute. Replacing them with a single average can lose that difference.

example.title: A phase pulse followed by a mixing pulse
steps: Start in |0⟩. Pulse A leaves |0⟩ fixed and multiplies |1⟩ by −i; pulse B is the matrix [[1,−i],[−i,1]]/√2.
Applying A then B gives (1,−i)/√2, whose plus-outcome chance is 1/2. The ordered product represents this sequence.

terms.definition: The state-change maps for the first and second pulses.
The operation for the whole sequence.
The normalized equal sum of |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.
To give the same result in either order. Two matrices commute when AB equals BA.

conserved-observables.idea: A quantity is conserved when its measured average stays fixed for every allowed starting state in this model.
conserved-observables.explanation: One lucky example with a fixed average is too little evidence. For a closed system, compare the time-independent measurement rule with its energy rule. If applying them in either order gives the same result, the quantity is conserved.

example.title: An accidentally constant average
steps: The fixed two-state energy rule turns the second component’s relative phase by −ωt. Starting in |0⟩ gives mean X = 0 at all times.
Starting with equal amplitudes instead gives mean X = cos(ωt). Thus one constant result does not make X generally conserved.

terms.definition: Hamiltonian, the energy operator.
The observable being checked.
HA − AH.
The energy-gap angular frequency.
The observable that swaps the two reference coordinates.
Elapsed time.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

spin-preparation.idea: A spin measurement needs a direction as well as a prepared particle.
spin-preparation.explanation: Spin is a built-in quantum property. For a spin-half particle a meter aimed along one axis has two possible readings. A differently aimed meter tests a different question. A state that always gives one answer along its first axis may have both answers possible along the next.

example.title: A z-axis spin test
steps: Prepare amplitudes (√3/2,1/2) in the z basis.
The +z chance is 3/4 and the −z chance is 1/4. The mean ℏ/4 is not a possible single reading.

spin-preparation.equation: positive z chance = |a|²; negative z chance = |b|²

terms.definition: Amplitudes for the two z-axis outcomes.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

pauli-matrices.idea: Three small number tables help predict spin readings along three directions.
pauli-matrices.explanation: The directions are x, y and z. Each table, called a Pauli matrix, has two possible result labels, +1 and −1. Multiply these labels by ℏ/2 to put them in units of angular momentum. Combining tables in a different order can change the result.

example.title: Checking the y matrix
steps: The y Pauli matrix sends (1,0) to (0,i).
Applying it again returns (1,0), checking that its square is the identity.

terms.definition: Spin component along axis k.
The corresponding dimensionless Pauli matrix.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

spin-direction-eigenstates.idea: A spin meter turned to a new direction can give a new mix of outcomes.
spin-direction-eigenstates.explanation: Measure the angle between the direction used to prepare the spin and the direction of the meter. For a spin-half particle, use half that angle in the wave formula. Then square the size of each result to get its chance. The physical meter turns by the full angle.

example.title: An analyzer 120° from z
steps: Prepare +z and point the new analyzer 120° from +z.
Its positive outcome has chance cos²60° = 1/4.

terms.definition: Angle between the analyzer’s axis n and positive z.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

bloch-pure-state.idea: One drawing can show the average spin results for three meter directions.
bloch-pure-state.explanation: Draw an arrow whose three coordinates are the averages along x, y and z. This is a Bloch arrow. It summarizes a state’s predictions. Point a meter along the arrow of a pure spin state and its positive outcome is certain.

example.title: A specified spin preparation
steps: For amplitudes (√3/2,i/2), the Bloch arrow has z-component 1/2.
The +z chance is (1 + 1/2)/2 = 3/4.

terms.definition: The Bloch vector of three Pauli averages.
The analyzer’s unit direction vector.
Dot product, comparing the directions and sizes of vectors.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

spinor-rotation.idea: A full turn of a spin-half state adds a minus sign to its wave description.
spinor-rotation.explanation: If this whole state is measured by itself, squaring its size removes the sign, so the chances stay the same. A comparison with another part of a wave that did not turn is different. Their minus sign is now relative and can change interference.

example.title: One full turn
steps: Rotate an initial +x spin-half state through 2π about z.
Its vector becomes the negative of the original, but a +x test still succeeds with certainty.

terms.definition: The ideal spin-rotation operator.
The identity operator, which leaves a vector unchanged.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.

magnetic-precession.idea: A spin’s average direction can circle a steady magnetic field.
magnetic-precession.explanation: This turning is called precession. Think of successive measurements on many particles prepared the same way. Their average traces the turning pattern. The sign of the particle’s magnetic response tells which way round that average moves.

example.title: Turning from x to y
steps: Use response γ = −4 radians/(second·tesla), field B_z = 0.5 tesla, and time t = π/4 seconds.
The angle is −γB_zt = π/2. An initial +x average points along +y.

terms.definition: Turning angle.
Signed magnetic response per field.
The z-directed field.
Elapsed time.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

two-level-hamiltonian.idea: Adding the same energy to two levels leaves the distance between them unchanged.
two-level-hamiltonian.explanation: If two readings each rise by 3, subtracting them still gives the old gap. In a two-state energy table, take out the common shift first. It changes the same phase of both wave parts. The remaining entries decide the gap and the states with definite energies.

example.title: A two-level energy matrix
steps: For H = E₀[[9,3],[3,1]], the common offset is 5E₀ and the splitting size is 5E₀.
The two energies are 5E₀ ± 5E₀: zero and 10E₀.

terms.definition: The shared energy offset.
The positive splitting size.
The two allowed energies.
The energy matrix.
A positive reference energy.

coupled-state-oscillations.idea: A repeating drive can move the chance of detection from one state to another and back again.
coupled-state-oscillations.explanation: A coupling is a link that lets the two states affect each other. At resonance the drive matches the energy separation. The chance of each outcome can then rise and fall in turn, while their total stays one.

example.title: Half a transfer
steps: Start in |0⟩ with coupling rate Ω = 4 radians per second.
At t = π/8 seconds, the |1⟩ chance is sin²(π/4) = 1/2.

terms.definition: The constant coupling rate.
Elapsed time.

detuning-and-avoided-crossing.idea: A drive that misses the matching frequency may never transfer the whole chance into the other state.
detuning-and-avoided-crossing.explanation: Detuning measures how far the drive is from the frequency matching the gap between energy levels. Both this mismatch and the link between the states affect the speed of the back-and-forth motion. The mismatch also sets a limit on how much can transfer.

example.title: A detuned pair
steps: Use detuning Δ = 3 and coupling Ω = 4 radians per second.
The largest transfer is Ω²/(Δ² + Ω²) = 16/25, or 64%.

terms.definition: Detuning: uncoupled energy difference divided by ℏ.
Coupling rate.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.

lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The gap is 5ℏ per second ≈5.27286×10⁻³⁴ J. At Δ=0 with the same coupling it narrows to 4ℏ per second.

rotating-frame-bridge.idea: Something spinning can look steady if you turn along with it.
rotating-frame-bridge.explanation: Watch a field rotating at 9 radians per second from coordinates turning the same way at 6. It appears to turn at 3. The same subtraction belongs in the energy rule when we describe a driven quantum system with turning coordinates.

example.title: A circular drive
steps: The system rate is 9 radians per second and the coordinates turn at 6.
Their difference is 3 radians per second. With coupling 4, the maximum transfer is 16/25.

terms.definition: Detuning in the rotating description.
The undriven system’s angular frequency.
The coordinate rotation and drive angular frequency.

rabi-approximation.idea: A rapidly changing part of a drive may mostly cancel out over the time you watch.
rabi-approximation.explanation: Near resonance, the drive nearly matches the frequency set by the energy gap. One contribution then builds up slowly while the other runs through many positive and negative parts. The rotating-wave approximation keeps the slow contribution when the link is weak and the timing supports this cancellation.

example.title: A weak resonant drive
steps: Drive and system frequencies are both 200 radians per second; coupling Ω is 2.
The approximation predicts complete transfer after π/Ω = π/2 seconds.

terms.definition: The near-resonant coupling angular rate.
A pulse intended to transfer the population completely in this approximation.
A result close enough to use when the stated conditions hold. For example, treating a nearly flat road as level can simplify a short-trip calculation.

coherent-number-expansion.idea: A quantum oscillator can have a well-defined wave pattern but several possible energy readings.
coherent-number-expansion.explanation: An oscillator has equally spaced energy steps. A coherent state gives particular chances for finding zero, one, two or more steps above the minimum. Their pattern, called a Poisson distribution, is set by the average number of steps. Include the chance of higher counts when adding the total.

example.title: Coherent amplitude one
steps: For α = 1, counts 0 and 1 each have probability e⁻¹; count 2 has probability e⁻¹/2.
These add to about 0.9197. Higher counts carry the remaining probability.

terms.definition: Nonnegative excitation count.
The mean count, |α|².
The product 1 × 2 × … × n, with 0! = 1.
The complex amplitude labeling the coherent state.
The number about 2.718 used for exponential change.
Probability of count n.
The count probabilities given by the displayed formula.

displacement-operator.idea: A quantum oscillator’s wave can be shifted without changing its width.
displacement-operator.explanation: Start with its lowest-energy state, sometimes called the vacuum. Here “vacuum” means zero added energy steps in this oscillator. A mathematical displacement changes its average position or momentum. Its spread stays equal to that of the starting state.

example.title: Displacing the vacuum
steps: Choose a real coherent amplitude α = 0.5. The displacement creates a coherent state from the lowest-energy state.
Its average excitation count is |α|² = 0.25, while its spread in position remains the ground-state spread.

terms.definition: The displacement operation.
The oscillator vacuum or lowest-energy state.
The coherent state with amplitude α.
The complex number specifying the displacement.
A number that sets how far the oscillator is shifted from its lowest-energy state and the stage of its cycle. Its squared size gives the average number of excitations.

coherent-quadratures.idea: Changing a wave’s average location can leave its spread exactly as wide as before.
coherent-quadratures.explanation: For this oscillator, the two quadratures are position and momentum measured in chosen units that remove their unit labels. In a coherent state the average of either can shift. Its variance, the average squared distance from its mean, stays at one half in these units.

example.title: A displaced coherent state
steps: Set α = 1 + i/2. The two quadrature averages are √2 and 1/√2.
Both variances remain 1/2; an average and a width are different quantities.

terms.definition: Dimensionless position and momentum quadratures.
The average squared distance from the mean.
The coherent-state amplitude.
Variance of the named quantity.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

coherent-evolution.idea: A bell-shaped quantum wave can move back and forth while keeping its width.
coherent-evolution.explanation: This is a coherent state of an ideal oscillator. A complex number tracks its average position and momentum. Its place around a circle changes as time passes, while its distance from the centre stays fixed. The motion describes averages for repeated measurements.

example.title: A quarter-cycle evolution
steps: Start with real coherent amplitude α₀ = 1.5. After phase ωt = π/2, the amplitude is −1.5i.
The mean count remains |α|² = 2.25.

terms.definition: Initial coherent amplitude.
Oscillator angular frequency.
Elapsed time.
Coherent amplitude at elapsed time t.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A number that sets how far the oscillator is shifted from its lowest-energy state and the stage of its cycle. Its squared size gives the average number of excitations.

coherent-number-comparison.idea: Equal average energy does not mean two preparations are the same.
coherent-number-comparison.explanation: A number state has one definite excitation count. A coherent state with the same average count has a spread of counts and different phase-sensitive predictions.

example.title: Two preparations with mean count two
steps: Compare number state |2⟩ with coherent amplitude √2. Both have mean energy 2.5ℏω.
The number state’s count variance is zero; the coherent state’s is two.

terms.definition: The state with exactly two excitations.
One oscillator energy spacing.
A number that sets how far the oscillator is shifted from its lowest-energy state and the stage of its cycle. Its squared size gives the average number of excitations.

tensor-basis.idea: For two systems, one label for each gives a label for the pair.
tensor-basis.explanation: If the first system can be 0 or 1 and so can the second, list 00, 01, 10 and 11. When the systems are independently prepared in pure states, multiply their individual wave amplitudes for each pair. A more general joint state need not come from two separate lists.

example.title: Two two-state systems
steps: A has probabilities 0.75 and 0.25; B has 0.60 and 0.40 in a product state.
In order 00,01,10,11, the joint probabilities are 0.45,0.30,0.15,0.10.

terms.definition: Amplitudes for the local labels i and j.
Their joint-label amplitude.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

local-operator-tensor.idea: A mathematical rule can change one member of a pair and leave the other member alone.
local-operator-tensor.explanation: A tensor product is a way to keep both labels together. A rule written as A ⊗ I acts on the first partner. The I means leave the second partner alone. Two rules that each act on a different partner give the same result in either order.

example.title: Swapping the first label
steps: Use joint order 00,01,10,11 and vector (1,2,3,4)/√30.
Swapping only the first system gives (3,4,1,2)/√30.

terms.definition: Operations on the first and second systems.
The identity, leaving that partner unchanged.
Combines the two systems’ spaces or operations.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.

lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: X flips the local 0/1 labels; Z gives signs +1 and −1.

joint-measurements.idea: There are two ways to ask about one partner in a pair. Did we keep every trial, or only some?
joint-measurements.explanation: To ignore the other partner’s reading, add the chances for all of its possible readings. To keep only trials with one particular reading, divide each matching joint chance by the chance of that reading. This requires a group with a nonzero chance of being selected.

example.title: Reading a joint table
steps: The probabilities for 00,01,10,11 are 0.5,0.2,0.1,0.2.
The chance that A is zero is 0.5 + 0.2 = 0.7, including either B outcome.

joint-measurements.equation: local chance = sum of joint chances over the other partner’s outcomes

terms.definition: The first and second systems’ outcome labels.
A local chance found by summing over the other system.

composite-hamiltonian.idea: An interaction can make the state of a pair impossible to describe with two separate pure states.
composite-hamiltonian.explanation: A rule acting independently on each partner preserves separate descriptions if they were separate at the start. A link between partners can change how the parts of their joint wave line up. If the resulting pure state cannot be split into separate states, it is entangled.

example.title: A phase interaction between two plus states
steps: Start with |+⟩⊗|+⟩. The Z⊗Z interaction gives opposite phases to matching and different labels.
At interaction phase π/4, the product-test sides are −i/4 and +i/4. They differ, so the state is entangled even though all four basis chances remain 1/4.

terms.definition: The four amplitudes in order 00,01,10,11.
Unable to split a pure joint state into one state per partner.
The normalized equal sum of |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The matrix that leaves |0⟩ fixed and reverses the sign of |1⟩.
Combine the two partners’ states or operations.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

lessonCopy.body.1: An interaction can instead depend on both labels. Use H_int=g Z⊗Z, with real g an energy and Z=diag(1,−1). This diagonal Hamiltonian gives energy +g to 00 and 11, and −g to 01 and 10. Define θ=gt/ℏ. Starting with |+⟩⊗|+⟩, where |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2, the evolved column is (e^(−iθ),e^(iθ),e^(iθ),e^(−iθ))ᵀ/2.
lessonCopy.body.2: A product column must satisfy c₀₀c₁₁=c₀₁c₁₀ because both sides multiply the same four local coefficients. At θ=π/4 the two sides are −i/4 and +i/4, so this preparation no longer factors. Interaction need not create entanglement at every time or for every input; at θ=π all four coefficients gain the same −1 phase and the original product returns. Define |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 to test other phase values by expanding a candidate product.

density-from-preparations.idea: A table can combine predictions for several randomly chosen ways of preparing a particle.
density-from-preparations.explanation: The table for one preparation is called a density matrix. If a coin chooses between two preparations, multiply each table by its chance of being chosen and add the tables. Adding their waves instead would describe a preparation with a definite connection between the waves.

example.title: Mixing zero and plus
steps: Prepare |0⟩ on 70% of runs and |+⟩ on 30%.
The plus-test chance is 0.70 × 0.5 + 0.30 × 1 = 0.65.

terms.definition: Density matrix describing the ensemble.
Chance of preparation j.
Its normalized state.
Add the listed contributions.
A table used to predict quantum measurement results. It can describe one prepared state or a random mixture of preparations.

trace-expectation.idea: A table of state information and a table for the meter together predict its average reading.
trace-expectation.explanation: First multiply the tables using the rules of matrix multiplication. Then add the entries down the main diagonal of the result. This diagonal sum is called the trace. Entries away from the diagonal in the original tables can affect the answer.

example.title: An energy expectation
steps: For the stated state and observable, the product’s diagonal entries are 1.45ε and 0.15ε.
Their sum is 1.60ε. With ε = 0.25 meV, the average is 0.40 meV.

trace-expectation.equation: average outcome = trace of (state matrix × observable matrix)

terms.definition: Add the diagonal entries after matrix multiplication.
The chosen energy unit.
One thousandth of an electronvolt.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.
A quantity a measurement can test, such as position or energy. In these calculations a mathematical rule represents it.

density-positivity.idea: A table that describes a quantum state must give a chance of zero or greater for every possible measurement outcome.
density-positivity.explanation: First check that the diagonal entries add to one and entries opposite each other across the diagonal are complex conjugates. A conjugate reverses the sign of the imaginary part. One more check matters. All the eigenvalues, or weights for independent states in that table, must be zero or positive.

example.title: A matrix that fails
steps: The matrix [[0.5,0.6],[0.6,0.5]] has trace one.
Its eigenvalues are 1.1 and −0.1, so it would assign a negative chance to one direction and cannot describe a state.

terms.definition: The multiplier for a direction left unchanged in shape by a matrix.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

lessonCopy.body.1: For a two-state system, write ρ=(I+r_x X+r_y Y+r_z Z)/2, where X,Y,Z are the Pauli matrices and r is a real three-component Bloch vector. With Y=[[0,−i],[i,0]], the matrix is [[1+r_z,r_x−ir_y],[r_x+ir_y,1−r_z]]/2. Its eigenvalues are (1+|r|)/2 and (1−|r|)/2. Validity therefore requires |r|≤1.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: The Hermitian matrix Q=[[0.5,0.6],[0.6,0.5]] has trace 1 but eigenvalues 1.1 and −0.1. In the |−⟩ direction it would predict −0.1, so it is not a state.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: The length is √(0.64+0.36)=1. The eigenvalues are (1±1)/2.

partial-trace.idea: A pair’s table of probabilities can be turned into a smaller table for just one partner.
partial-trace.explanation: Add together entries with matching labels for the partner being ignored. This procedure is called the partial trace. The smaller table predicts every measurement on the remaining partner alone. To predict how both partners’ results match, keep the whole joint table.

example.title: Adding over the partner’s labels
steps: Prepare √0.6|+0⟩ + i√0.4|−1⟩. The second label belongs to the ignored partner.
For the first partner, one diagonal entry is 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5; the off-diagonal entry is 0.3 − 0.2 = 0.1.
Its reduced matrix is [[0.5,0.1],[0.1,0.5]], containing all first-partner predictions.

partial-trace.equation: local matrix = sum over matching partner labels

terms.definition: A matrix containing all predictions for one partner alone.
The normalized equal plus and minus combinations of states 0 and 1.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

lessonCopy.body.2: As a concrete pure state, prepare |ψ⟩=√0.6|+⟩_A|0⟩_B+i√0.4|−⟩_A|1⟩_B. Its column is (√0.3,i√0.2,√0.3,−i√0.2). Form ρ_AB=|ψ⟩⟨ψ| first, then use the matching-index sum. Ignoring a partner’s results is a prediction rule, not a physical removal of that partner.
lessonCopy.visual.caption: Separate distinguishable-system pure family |ψ⟩=cosθ|00⟩+e^(iφ)sinθ|11⟩, with 0≤θ≤π/2. Controls compare joint preparations; they do not choose distant measurement outcomes. Angles are shown in degrees and converted to radians. Each local reduced state is diag(cos²θ,sin²θ), independent of the relative phase φ. Bars show joint x-basis probabilities in the stated order, with |±x⟩=(|0⟩±|1⟩)/√2; same-sign bars equal [1+sin(2θ)cosφ]/4 and opposite-sign bars equal [1−sin(2θ)cosφ]/4. Local purity is cos⁴θ+sin⁴θ. Probabilities, purity and Schmidt rank have no units. Phase can change correlations without changing either local state; changing θ changes the preparation weights themselves.

purity-and-unrecorded-measurement.idea: Losing a measurement result can leave a mixture of possible states.
purity-and-unrecorded-measurement.explanation: A pure state has one complete wave description. A mixture requires several possibilities with weights. For the normalized table here, a number called purity equals one for a pure state and is smaller for a mixture. Forgetting a result can lower it.

example.title: Ignoring a basis measurement
steps: Start in pure |+⟩, whose purity is one. Measure 0/1 and forget which result occurred.
The result is an equal mixture with purity 0.5. Selecting a recorded branch would be a different task.

terms.definition: The density matrix.
The sum of diagonal entries.
The normalized equal sum of |0⟩ and |1⟩.

lessonCopy.body.2: For |+⟩, the density is [[0.5,0.5],[0.5,0.5]]. An ignored 0/1 measurement produces diag(0.5,0.5), whose purity is 0.5. If result 0 is actually recorded and selected, the conditioned state is |0⟩⟨0| with purity 1; that subensemble has probability 0.5. Ignoring and selecting are different operations.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: Apply U=diag(1,i) to pure |+⟩. The state becomes (|0⟩+i|1⟩)/√2 and its density has off-diagonal entries −i/2 and +i/2. Its purity remains 1.

product-or-entangled.idea: A pure state of a pair is entangled if its numbers cannot be made from two separate lists.
product-or-entangled.explanation: For two systems with two choices each, place the four wave amplitudes in a two-by-two table. Multiply the two diagonal entries and subtract the product of the other two. If that number, the determinant, is nonzero, the pure pair cannot split into independent states.

example.title: Testing four amplitudes
steps: Use coefficient matrix [[1,2],[2,1]]/√10.
Its determinant is (1 − 4)/10 = −0.3, so this pure state is entangled.

terms.definition: The amplitude for joint label ij.
A pure joint state that cannot factor into one state per partner.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

lessonCopy.example.steps.1: Changing the coefficients to C=(1/√10)[[1,2],[2,1]] keeps the norm 1 but gives determinant (1−4)/10=−0.3. This pure state is entangled.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: Both diagonal coefficients are nonzero, giving determinant √0.09=0.3; normalization alone does not imply factorization.

schmidt-decomposition.idea: A pure quantum pair can be described using matched pairs of reference states.
schmidt-decomposition.explanation: Choose a special set of reference states for each partner and match the first with the first, the second with the second, and so on. This is the Schmidt form. If only one pair has nonzero weight, each partner has its own pure state. If several have weight, the pair is entangled.

example.title: Two matched pairs
steps: Write the state as √0.75|+0⟩ + √0.25|−1⟩.
The weights 0.75 and 0.25 are both positive, so its Schmidt rank is two and it is entangled.

terms.definition: Positive weights summing to one.
Matched orthonormal reference states for the two partners.
The number of positive weights.
The pure joint state.
Add all matched-pair terms.
Combine the two local states into a joint product.
The equal plus and minus combinations of |0⟩ and |1⟩.

lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The reduced matrix is ρ_A=[[0.5,0.25],[0.25,0.5]]. Its eigenvectors |+⟩ and |−⟩ have eigenvalues 0.75 and 0.25. Contracting with their bras and dividing by √0.75 or √0.25 returns B partners |0⟩ and |1⟩.

two-spin-correlations.idea: Two particles can each give random spin readings while their results form a definite pattern together.
two-spin-correlations.explanation: In a state called the singlet, the two spin-half particles have total spin zero. Aim both meters in the same direction and the two readings are opposite. Turn one meter, and the pattern of agreement changes with the angle.

example.title: Matching analyzer directions
steps: Measure both singlet partners along z.
Each side sees plus half the time, but the two results are always opposite in this ideal model.

terms.definition: The two unit analyzer directions.
Mean product of the ±1 outcome labels.
The antisymmetric pair (|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2.
Dot product; for unit vectors it equals the cosine of their angle.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
Individual outcomes can vary even when you repeat the same setup.

lessonCopy.body.1: For unit directions a and b, define A=a·σ and B=b·σ, where a·σ=a_xX+a_yY+a_zZ. Their outcomes are ±1; the physical spin outcomes are ±ℏ/2. Direct Pauli products in this state give ⟨σ_i⊗σ_j⟩=−δ_ij, where δ_ij is 1 for matching Cartesian directions and 0 otherwise. Expanding the two sums gives E(a,b)=⟨A⊗B⟩=−a·b.
lessonCopy.body.2: The projectors for outcome s=±1 along a are (I+s a·σ)/2. Expanding the pair of projectors gives P(s,t)=[1−st a·b]/4, since both local means vanish. Equal directions give only opposite results; perpendicular directions give all four outcomes equally often. These are joint statistics of this preparation, not predetermined classical arrows attached to each spin.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: Choose axes separated by 30 degrees, θ=π/6. Then E=−√3/2≈−0.866025. Each same-sign pair has probability (1−√3/2)/4≈0.0334936.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The total same-sign probability is about 0.0669873; different signs total about 0.933013. Those totals add to 1. Physical spin-product expectation is −(√3/8)ℏ² for this angle.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: S_a=(ℏ/2)a·σ; the physical product has units (J·s)².

bell-chsh-bound.idea: Comparing two distant sets of spin readings can test a rule about where their answers come from.
bell-chsh-bound.explanation: Each meter can choose between two settings. The CHSH test combines four measures of how often the two readings agree. If each answer depends only on its own setting and shared earlier information, with independent setting choices and fair sampling, the combined size is at most 2. Some quantum states exceed 2.

example.title: The stated four analyzer settings
steps: The four correlations are −1/√2, −1/√2, −1/√2 and +1/√2.
Their CHSH combination is −2√2, whose magnitude about 2.828 exceeds the stated local-model bound of 2.

terms.definition: A correlation: mean product of the two ±1 results.
Two analyzer choices on each side.
The CHSH combination.

lessonCopy.body.0: Consider a shared variable λ with a normalized probability distribution independent of which measurement settings are chosen. In a deterministic local-response description, A(a,λ), A(a′,λ), B(b,λ), B(b′,λ) are each ±1. A’s response depends on its own setting and λ, not B’s chosen setting; B obeys the analogous condition. Local stochastic responses also obey the bound, by averaging deterministic responses or by using conditional means between −1 and 1.
lessonCopy.body.1: For one λ, form C=A(B+B′)+A′(B−B′). Since B and B′ are ±1, either B+B′ is ±2 and B−B′ is 0, or the reverse. Thus C is ±2. Averaging with the same setting-independent distribution gives |S|≤2, where S=E(a,b)+E(a,b′)+E(a′,b)−E(a′,b′). The four correlations must refer to the specified common preparation and sampling rule; setting-dependent or outcome-dependent discarded events cannot silently be treated as that same model.
lessonCopy.body.2: Quantum correlations of the preceding state give E=−a·b. Choose axes in the x-z plane with n(θ)=(sinθ,0,cosθ). Use a at 20°, a′ at 110°, b at 65° and b′ at −25°. A degree angle converts to radians by multiplying by π/180. The relative angles are −45°,45°,45°,135°, giving a quantum value whose magnitude exceeds 2. This rules out the stated combined local-response and setting-independence model for those ideal statistics; it is not a blanket refutation of every interpretation or a signalling protocol.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: The four quantum correlations for the stated axes are −1/√2,−1/√2,−1/√2,+1/√2. Their signed combination is S=−2√2≈−2.828427.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For a contrasting set with all four axes equal, all four E values are −1 and S=−2. A quantum state need not violate this inequality for every choice of settings.

local-no-signalling.idea: Without the other observer’s results, one observer cannot see a change caused only by the distant observer choosing a measurement.
local-no-signalling.explanation: The distant result can sort local readings into groups with different averages. But until the observers share their records, all the groups are mixed together. Their weighted average gives the same local predictions as before.

example.title: Ignoring a remote singlet result
steps: A remote z-plus result selects local z-minus; remote z-minus selects local z-plus. Each has probability 1/2.
Without the record, the local plus chance remains 1/2.

local-no-signalling.equation: local state after ignored remote measurement = original local state

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For |Ψ⁻⟩, B obtains z-plus with probability 1/2. Given that result, A is |1⟩ and its Z mean is −1. B’s other result selects |0⟩ with Z mean +1.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: Ignoring the record gives mean (1/2)(−1)+(1/2)(+1)=0 and P_A(0)=1/2. If B instead measures X, its plus result selects |−⟩ on A, whose Z mean is 0; the unconditioned A state is again I/2.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: In the different pure state √0.8|00⟩+√0.2|11⟩, an ignored B measurement in the 0/1 basis leaves A’s probabilities 0.8 and 0.2 unchanged. Selecting B=1 has probability 0.2 and then A=1 with certainty.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: z-plus is |0⟩; x-plus is |+⟩. No outcome is assumed controllable by choosing the measurement basis.

angular-ladder-spectrum.idea: Angular momentum along one chosen direction takes separate steps.
angular-ladder-spectrum.explanation: The label j names the total angular momentum. The label m picks one allowed component along the chosen axis. A raising rule increases m by one while keeping j fixed. At the highest allowed m the rule gives zero, so no extra state appears.

example.title: Raising a spin-three-halves state
steps: Start at j = 3/2, m = 1/2.
Raising gives √3ℏ times the m = 3/2 state. Another raising step gives zero.

terms.definition: Total angular-momentum label.
Chosen component label.
The raising operator.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: The two factors are 1 and 4, not 1 and 2.

spin-one-matrices.idea: A definite spin-one component can leave another component uncertain.
spin-one-matrices.explanation: Spin one uses three basis states rather than spin half’s two. The matrix for a component may mix those basis states, so a sharp x result need not give a sharp z result.

example.title: A definite positive x state
steps: In z-basis order +1,0,−1, prepare (1/2,1/√2,1/2).
The x result is certainly +ℏ, but z outcomes have chances 1/4,1/2,1/4.

terms.definition: Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.
A grid of numbers. In these calculations it can act as a rule that turns one list of numbers into another.

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Multiply J_x by (1/2,1/√2,1/2)ᵀ. The result is ℏ times the same vector, verifying the +ℏ eigenvalue.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For the middle basis vector (0,1,0)ᵀ, J_x produces (ℏ/√2)(1,0,1)ᵀ. Its norm squared is ℏ², so this preparation has ⟨J_x²⟩=ℏ² and ⟨J_x⟩=0.

orbital-rotation-action.idea: To turn a wave pattern, shift where you look up its old values.
orbital-rotation-action.explanation: Imagine turning a drawing clockwise. To find the color at a new point, trace that point back counterclockwise on the old drawing. A rotated spatial wave is calculated the same way. A particle’s built-in spin needs its own rotation rule as well.

example.title: A quarter-turn of an orbital shape
steps: Begin with the normalized angular shape Y_x. Rotate it 90° about z.
The result is Y_y, with the same radial dependence and normalization.

terms.definition: Position vector.
Orthogonal orbital angular shapes oriented along x and y.
Position amplitudes before and after the rotation.
The inverse rotation, undoing R.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

lessonCopy.body.1: For a small positive rotation α about z, R⁻¹ sends (x,y) to approximately (x+αy,y−αx). Expanding a smooth function gives ψ_rot≈ψ+α(y∂_x−x∂_y)ψ. This equals (I−iαL_z/ℏ)ψ for L_z=−iℏ(x∂_y−y∂_x). It checks both the generator and its sign.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: For α=π/3, the angular state is (1/2)Y_x+(√3/2)Y_y. A projector onto Y_x has probability 1/4, and onto Y_y probability 3/4.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For a small α, the Y_y amplitude starts at approximately α while the Y_x amplitude changes only at second order. This agrees with the generator’s first derivative.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: α rotates about +z; θ is measured from +z, φ from +x toward +y.

angular-rotation-matrices.idea: Turning a spin state changes the chances of meter readings along a fixed axis.
angular-rotation-matrices.explanation: For a spin-one particle there are three possible readings along that axis. A rotation mixes their wave amplitudes within the same three-state group. Add the amplitudes using the rotation table, then square their sizes to get the new chances.

example.title: A 90° spin-one rotation
steps: Start with z-component +ℏ and rotate 90° about y.
The z-basis amplitudes become (1/2,1/√2,1/2), giving chances 1/4,1/2,1/4.

terms.definition: Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

lessonCopy.body.0: In the j=1 basis (m=+1,0,−1), use U_y(α)=exp(−iαJ_y/ℏ). Since J_y/ℏ has eigenvalues +1,0,−1, its exponential can be obtained from the three spectral projectors. Write c=cosα and s=sinα for compact entries.
lessonCopy.body.1: The resulting real matrix is [[(1+c)/2,−s/√2,(1−c)/2],[s/√2,c,−s/√2],[(1−c)/2,s/√2,(1+c)/2]]. It is orthogonal and therefore unitary. Its derivative at α=0 equals −iJ_y/ℏ, confirming the signs against the generator.
lessonCopy.body.2: Apply it to the highest-weight input (1,0,0)ᵀ. The output is ((1+c)/2,s/√2,(1−c)/2)ᵀ. The three J_z probabilities are the squares of those real coefficients. The J² value stays 2ℏ² because rotations remain inside the same j multiplet.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: At α=π/2, the output is (1/2,1/√2,1/2)ᵀ, the earlier J_x=+ℏ state. The J_z probabilities are 1/4,1/2,1/4.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: At α=π, the output is (0,0,1)ᵀ. The J_z value is certainly −ℏ, while J² is still 2ℏ².
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For a small α, the middle amplitude is approximately α/√2, so its probability starts as α²/2. A first-order amplitude change can create a second-order probability change.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: The sine square is 3/4, but the amplitude also contains 1/√2.

angular-expectation-spread.idea: The average of squared readings can differ from the square of their average.
angular-expectation-spread.explanation: For instance, +1 and −1 average to zero, but their squares both equal one. The same distinction matters for angular momentum. The difference measures the spread of the readings. Squaring only the averages would throw away that information.

example.title: A rotated spin-one state
steps: At rotation angle π/3, the squared mean-vector length is ℏ², while the total-square value is 2ℏ².
The component variances add to ℏ², exactly the missing amount.

angular-expectation-spread.equation: mean total square − squared mean-vector length = sum of component variances

terms.definition: The average squared deviation from the mean.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A list of components that can be added and scaled together. A familiar example is a displacement arrow with length and direction.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

lessonCopy.body.2: The mean-vector squared length is j²ℏ², while ⟨J²⟩=j(j+1)ℏ². Their difference equals the sum of component variances, jℏ². For x and y, the uncertainty product is σ_xσ_y=(jℏ²/2)|cosα|, equal to (ℏ/2)|⟨J_z⟩| for this prepared family.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Use j=1 and α=π/3. The mean components in units of ℏ are (√3/2,0,1/2). Their squared length is 1, while the J² eigenvalue in units of ℏ² is 2.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The variances in units of ℏ² are 1/8,1/2,3/8. They add to 1, exactly the difference between mean square and squared mean.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The x-y uncertainty product is √[(1/8)(1/2)]ℏ²=ℏ²/4. Its commutator lower bound is (ℏ/2)|ℏ/2|=ℏ²/4, so this state saturates that bound.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.0.label: Mean J_z in units of ℏ
lessonCopy.practice.parts.1.label: J_y variance in units of ℏ²
lessonCopy.practice.parts.2.label: J_x variance in units of ℏ²
lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.label: J² eigenvalue in units of ℏ²
lessonCopy.practice.reasoning: Contrast the squared mean-vector length 4ℏ² with the invariant 6ℏ² and account for their difference. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

total-angular-operators.idea: Two angular momenta combine differently depending on how their directions are linked.
total-angular-operators.explanation: To find the possible totals, add the rules for the two angular momenta first, then square the sum. The extra term involves both together. It explains how two particles with the same individual spin sizes can still have different combined spin values.

example.title: Two spin-half partners
steps: Each partner has spin label 1/2. Their four-dimensional joint space splits into total j = 1 and j = 0.
These contain three and one states, preserving the total of four.

terms.definition: The two partners’ angular-momentum operators.
Their total operator.
Dot product: add products of matching components.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For two spin-one-half factors, the product space has dimension 2×2=4. Allowed total j values are 1 and 0, contributing 3+1=4 coupled states.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: For j₁=1 and j₂=1/2, allowed total j values are 3/2 and 1/2. Their dimensions 4+2 again equal the product dimension 3×2=6.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For two spin-one-half states with total j=1, the dot product eigenvalue is (ℏ²/2)[2−3/4−3/4]=ℏ²/4. For total j=0 it is −3ℏ²/4. The same individual spins permit different correlations.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: Unit steps from 1/2 to 3/2 give only 1/2 and 3/2.
lessonCopy.apply.answer: No. The cross term 2J₁·J₂ is generally nonzero and can differ between coupled sectors. For example, it distinguishes the singlet and triplet of two spin-one-half systems even though both individual squared spins are fixed.

singlet-triplet.idea: Two spin-half systems have one total-spin-zero state and three total-spin-one states.
singlet-triplet.explanation: The one state is called the singlet. The three are called the triplet. When the two individual readings could be opposite, their wave contributions can combine with a plus or minus sign. That sign decides which group the combination belongs to.

example.title: An opposite-spin product
steps: The product |+−⟩ is an equal sum of the zero-component triplet and singlet.
Measuring total angular-momentum square gives 2ℏ² or zero, each with probability 1/2.

terms.definition: A state labeled by total angular momentum j and its component M.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

lessonCopy.body.0: Use |+⟩ and |−⟩ for each subsystem’s S_z=±ℏ/2 states. The ordered product basis is (|++⟩,|+−⟩,|−+⟩,|−−⟩). The highest total component M=1 has the unique state |++⟩; it belongs to total j=1.
lessonCopy.body.1: Applying the total lowering operator gives ℏ(|−+⟩+|+−⟩). Dividing by its norm √2ℏ produces |1,0⟩=(|+−⟩+|−+⟩)/√2. Lower once more to obtain |1,−1⟩=|−−⟩. These three j=1 states are the triplet.
lessonCopy.body.2: The remaining orthogonal state is |0,0⟩=(|+−⟩−|−+⟩)/√2. Both total raising and lowering annihilate it, and J_z also gives zero; therefore J² gives zero. This single j=0 state is the singlet.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: The overlap between the two M=0 combinations is (1−1)/2=0, and each has norm one.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: An initial product |+−⟩ equals (|1,0⟩+|0,0⟩)/√2. Measuring J² yields 2ℏ² or 0 with probability 1/2 each, while J_z is certainly zero.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.0.description: The first symbol labels subsystem 1 and the second subsystem 2. Each single-spin component is ±ℏ/2.

unequal-angular-addition.idea: Two different-sized spins can combine into more than one possible total spin.
unequal-angular-addition.explanation: Start with the state that has the largest possible reading along your chosen axis. Lower its reading one step to build a combination in the same total-spin family. Another combination with zero overlap can belong to a different family. Keep the signs when forming each wave.

example.title: Combining spin one and spin half
steps: For total j = 3/2 and component M = 1/2, the two product amplitudes are √(2/3) and √(1/3).
The corresponding component pairs occur with probabilities 2/3 and 1/3.

terms.definition: Total angular momentum and its component.
The first and second systems’ component labels.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

lessonCopy.body.0: Combine j₁=1 with j₂=1/2. Write |m₁,m₂⟩ for the product states and |j,M⟩ for coupled states, with fixed j₁,j₂ understood. The unique highest state is |3/2,3/2⟩=|1,+1/2⟩.
lessonCopy.body.1: The total lowering operator produces √2ℏ|0,+1/2⟩+ℏ|1,−1/2⟩. The coupled lowering coefficient is √3ℏ, so |3/2,1/2⟩=√(2/3)|0,+1/2⟩+√(1/3)|1,−1/2⟩.
lessonCopy.body.2: In this two-dimensional M=1/2 subspace, a normalized orthogonal vector is |1/2,1/2⟩=√(1/3)|0,+1/2⟩−√(2/3)|1,−1/2⟩. Raising it gives zero, verifying that it is the highest state of the j=1/2 multiplet. This choice fixes an overall phase convention for that multiplet.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The overlap of the two displayed coupled states is √2/3−√2/3=0. Their norms are each 2/3+1/3=1.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: Raising the j=1/2 combination gives [√(1/3)√2−√(2/3)]ℏ|1,+1/2⟩=0. This checks the relative minus sign independently of the norm.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.0: Correct. Its overlap magnitude with the displayed j=1/2 state is √(2/3).

coupled-basis-measurements.idea: A total-spin measurement can change later individual-spin chances.
coupled-basis-measurements.explanation: A product preparation can contain several total-spin components. Selecting one component keeps a different state, so the next measurement must use that new preparation.

example.title: Two selected outcomes
steps: Start with individual labels (0,+1/2). The total j = 3/2 outcome has probability 2/3.
After selecting it, first-system label +1 has probability 1/3. Both results occur with chance 2/9.

terms.definition: A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.
One part of a quantity after you choose directions or reference patterns. A displacement may have an eastward part and a northward part.

lessonCopy.body.0: Use the j₁=1,j₂=1/2 pair and prepare the product |0,+1/2⟩. It expands as √(2/3)|3/2,1/2⟩+√(1/3)|1/2,1/2⟩. This equation describes one preparation in two bases; no measurement has happened yet.
lessonCopy.body.1: An ideal total-J² measurement selects one coupled multiplet. The j=3/2 outcome has probability 2/3. Conditioned on it, the state is |3/2,1/2⟩, which has product-basis weights 2/3 for |0,+1/2⟩ and 1/3 for |1,−1/2⟩.
lessonCopy.body.2: Therefore the joint probability of first selecting j=3/2 and then finding m₁=1 is (2/3)(1/3)=2/9. Without the intervening total-J² measurement, the initial product state had m₁=0 certainly. Conditioning changed the later preparation.
lessonCopy.body.3: The total component M remains 1/2 throughout these selected branches, but total j and individual m₁ are different observable labels. They cannot all be treated as fixed classical labels of the original state.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For initial |0,+1/2⟩, the two total-J² eigenvalues are (15/4)ℏ² and (3/4)ℏ² with probabilities 2/3 and 1/3.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.2: Correct. The first chance is 1/3 and the conditional m₁=0 chance is 1/3, giving 1/9.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.0.description: The fixed pair is j₁=1,j₂=1/2, and M=m₁+m₂. Component values include a factor ℏ.

spin-orbit-energy.idea: The energy of an atom can depend on how spin and orbital motion line up.
spin-orbit-energy.explanation: Spin is the electron’s built-in angular momentum. Its wave pattern around the nucleus has orbital angular momentum. Their interaction, called spin–orbit coupling, can split an energy level. How large the split is depends on the atom as well as the angular labels.

example.title: A specified positive coupling
steps: For l = 1, s = 1/2 and λ = 0.020 eV, the two shifts are +0.010 and −0.020 eV.
Their separation is 0.030 eV in this effective model.

terms.definition: The supplied coupling-energy scale.
Orbital, spin and total angular labels.
The energy shift of the total-angular-momentum family j.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

lessonCopy.body.0: Consider H_int=λL·S/ℏ², where λ is a stated energy and L,S are orbital and spin angular operators. The factor ℏ² removes the angular units, leaving energy. This is a specified effective coupling; we are not deriving atomic fine structure here.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The two sectors have 4 and 2 M states. Their degeneracy-weighted mean shift is [4(λ/2)+2(−λ)]/6=0.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For λ=−0.020 eV, the two shifts become −0.010 and +0.020 eV. The ordering reverses, but the positive separation remains 0.030 eV.
lessonCopy.practice.prompt: Use l=1,s=1/2 and λ=+0.030 eV. Separately prepare the uncoupled product |m₁=1,m₂=−1/2⟩ for the same angular pair.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.feedback: The corresponding coupled overlap has magnitude √(2/3).
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: Here l=1,s=1/2, so j=3/2 or 1/2. The s label is not seconds.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.3.description: Dividing L·S by ℏ² makes a dimensionless operator.

exchange-postulate.idea: Swapping the labels on two identical particles tells us about the shape of their shared wave.
exchange-postulate.explanation: Swap all the labels, including position and spin. In three dimensions, the full wave for identical bosons keeps its sign. For identical fermions it changes sign. These names describe two kinds of particles. The labels help calculate outcomes without tracking two permanent identities.

example.title: Exchanging a symmetric pair
steps: Use orthogonal modes a and b in (|a,b⟩ + |b,a⟩)/√2.
Swapping the slots reverses the order of the two terms but leaves the state unchanged.

exchange-postulate.equation: ΠΨ = +Ψ for bosons; ΠΨ = −Ψ for fermions

terms.definition: The complete-particle exchange operation.
The complete two-particle state.
Having zero overlap in the chosen way of comparing vectors or patterns. Ordinary arrows at right angles provide one example.

lessonCopy.body.2: The labels 1 and 2 identify tensor slots in the calculation, not permanent observable tags attached to two identical particles. Different species, such as an electron and proton, can be distinguished by their physical type and need not be symmetrized as one species.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For two distinct orthogonal modes a,b, the normalized combination (|a,b⟩+|b,a⟩)/√2 is unchanged by exchange.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The normalized difference (|a,b⟩−|b,a⟩)/√2 changes sign under exchange. Its probability density remains nonnegative because probabilities use magnitude squares.

symmetric-pair-normalization.idea: When two wave arrangements overlap, adding them can change the size by more than you might expect.
symmetric-pair-normalization.explanation: Combine one arrangement with the arrangement formed by swapping the particles. If they overlap, their waves can reinforce. To make all chances add to one, divide by the size of the whole sum. The usual divisor √2 works when the two one-particle states have zero overlap.

example.title: Two overlapping states
steps: Use u = |0⟩ and v = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩. Their overlap is 0.6.
The symmetric numerator’s squared norm is 2(1 + 0.6²) = 2.72, so divide by √2.72.

terms.definition: The overlap ⟨u|v⟩ of the normalized one-particle states.

lessonCopy.body.0: Let u and v be normalized one-particle states, with overlap S=⟨u|v⟩. The symmetric numerator is |u,v⟩+|v,u⟩. Its norm squared has two diagonal terms equal to one and two cross terms equal to |S|², so the total is 2(1+|S|²).
lessonCopy.body.1: The normalized boson pair is Ψ_+=(|u,v⟩+|v,u⟩)/√[2(1+|S|²)]. The familiar 1/√2 coefficient applies only when u and v are orthogonal. If they are identical, the numerator and denominator both contain the factor 2, leaving the normalized product |u,u⟩.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Use u=|0⟩ and v=0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩. Then S=0.6, and the normalizing denominator is √2.72≈1.64924.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The normalized numerator expanded in the ordered basis is 1.2|00⟩+0.8|01⟩+0.8|10⟩, divided by √2.72. The squared entries sum to (1.44+0.64+0.64)/2.72=1.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The probability that both detections occupy mode 0 is 1.44/2.72=9/17≈0.52941. The probability of one in each mode is 8/17; neither result comes from simply treating u,v as exclusive labels.
lessonCopy.check.prompt: Change v to (√3/2)|0⟩+(1/2)|1⟩ while keeping u=|0⟩. What is the denominator squared?
lessonCopy.check.explanations.2: That would require identical states with |S|²=1.
lessonCopy.apply.answer: No. The two cross terms are each |S|², which is real and nonnegative. A scalar phase affects amplitudes, but a norm is built with conjugation. Replacing |S|² by S² would be an error.

fermion-determinant.idea: Two identical fermions, such as two electrons, cannot share the same complete state.
fermion-determinant.explanation: The joint wave contains two assignments of the particle labels, with a minus sign between them. If both particles have exactly the same state, those two terms are equal and cancel. The proposed arrangement has no allowed wave.

example.title: One fermion in each mode
steps: Use orthogonal complete modes 0 and 1 in (|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2.
An occupation measurement always finds one in each mode; swapping slot names does not create a second arrangement.

terms.definition: Orthogonal complete one-particle states, including any spin label.
The antisymmetric two-fermion state.
Having zero overlap in the chosen way of comparing vectors or patterns. Ordinary arrows at right angles provide one example.

lessonCopy.body.2: The word complete matters: a spatial orbital together with spin labels is a single-particle state. Two electrons may share a spatial orbital if their complete spin-orbital states are different. The normalization 1/√2 here assumes u and v are orthonormal.
lessonCopy.body.3: In a finite two-mode basis with u=|0⟩,v=|1⟩, the ordered coefficients are (0,1/√2,−1/√2,0). Physical occupation measurements always find one fermion in each of those modes; tensor-slot labels are not particle identity tags.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For u=|0⟩,v=|1⟩, the two nonzero ordered amplitudes have squared weights 1/2 each, giving total norm one.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: Both correspond to the same physical occupation statement: one in each mode. The probabilities for two in mode 0 or two in mode 1 are zero.
lessonCopy.check.prompt: Use u=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and v=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 instead. What is the probability of one occupation in each original 0/1 mode?
lessonCopy.check.explanations.1: Its two ordered entries each have weight 1/2, but together they give the one-in-each occupation probability 1.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: The 2×2 determinant is ad−bc; its columns are one-particle states.

spin-spatial-symmetry.idea: Two electrons in the same spatial state need a particular combined spin state.
spin-spatial-symmetry.explanation: Swapping the labels of two electrons must change the sign of their full wave. If the spatial part stays the same, the spin part must supply the minus sign. For two electrons sharing one orbital, this selects the total-spin-zero pair called the singlet.

example.title: Two electrons in one orbital
steps: Both electrons use spatial orbital a, so the spatial product |a,a⟩ is symmetric.
Pair it with the spin singlet. The total exchange sign is (+1)(−1) = −1.

terms.definition: The antisymmetric spin pair (|+−⟩ − |−+⟩)/√2.
A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

lessonCopy.body.0: If a two-electron state factors into a spatial part φ and a spin part χ, exchanging complete particles exchanges both factors. Their signs multiply. A symmetric spatial factor must therefore pair with an antisymmetric spin factor, and an antisymmetric spatial factor with a symmetric spin factor.
lessonCopy.body.1: The spin singlet χ_s=(|+−⟩−|−+⟩)/√2 is antisymmetric. The three triplet states are symmetric. For orthonormal spatial orbitals a,b, spatial sums/differencesφ_±=(|a,b⟩±|b,a⟩)/√2 have the indicated signs.
lessonCopy.body.2: When both electrons occupy the same spatial orbital a, the spatial product |a,a⟩ is symmetric. The allowed factorized spin state is then the singlet. An unantisymmetrized product |+−⟩ alone is not the required complete two-electron state.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: For different orthonormal orbitals a,b, φ_+χ_s has complete exchange sign (+1)(−1)=−1 and is allowed for two electrons.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The spatial difference φ_- paired with the M=0 triplet has sign (−1)(+1)=−1 and is also allowed. Both singlet and this triplet have opposite individual z results, but their relative signs differ.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For the same spatial orbital a, the antisymmetric spatial difference is zero. The remaining normalized spatial product |a,a⟩ must pair with χ_s in this factorized setup.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: Their S_z outcomes are ±ℏ/2. Opposite z labels alone do not uniquely imply a singlet.

occupation-and-filling.idea: A list of how many particles occupy each state can replace a list of individual names.
occupation-and-filling.explanation: Each entry gives the number in one complete wave pattern, including any spin label. Identical fermions can have only zero or one in each such state. For independent particles, add up the energies of the filled states.

example.title: Two spinless fermions
steps: Two available complete modes have energies 1 eV and 3 eV.
With two spinless fermions, each mode must hold one, giving total energy 4 eV.

terms.definition: Number occupying complete mode j.
That mode’s one-particle energy.
Total energy in this noninteracting model.
Add over the modes.

lessonCopy.body.0: An occupation list (n₀,n₁,…) gives the number of particles in each orthonormal complete mode. Its entries sum to the fixed particle number N. Boson occupations can be 0,1,2,…; fermion occupations are 0 or 1 for each complete mode.
lessonCopy.body.1: For a noninteracting Hamiltonian with one-particle energies ε_j, the total energy is E=Σ_j n_jε_j. Interactions generally change this simple sum. A mode includes any spin label, so “one fermion per mode” is not automatically “one per spatial orbital.”
lessonCopy.body.2: With two spinless modes and N=2, bosons have three occupation lists:(2,0),(1,1),(0,2). Spinless fermions have only (1,1). Exchanging particle-slot names does not create a new occupation configuration.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Take two spinless modes with energies 1 eV and 3 eV and N=2. The three boson lists have energies 2,4 and 6 eV.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: For spinless fermions, only one particle in each listed mode is allowed, giving 4 eV. Reordering two slot labels does not add a second physical configuration.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For electrons with two spin modes per spatial orbital and negligible interactions, the four complete modes have energies 1,1,3,3 eV. Two electrons can fill the two lowest complete modes for energy 2 eV; their shared spatial orbital pairs with the spin singlet.
lessonCopy.check.prompt: Use three spinless modes with energies 0, 2 and 5 eV and two noninteracting fermions. What is the lowest allowed total energy?
lessonCopy.check.explanations.1: Correct. Fill the distinct 0 and 2 eV modes.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.2: Filling the 5 eV mode is not needed for two particles.

exchange-energy.idea: Two ways of combining the same pair of orbitals can give different average interaction energies.
exchange-energy.explanation: An orbital is a possible spatial wave for one particle. Make a pair by adding the two assignments of the orbitals or by subtracting them.
