Where the assignments overlap, their contributions can reinforce or cancel. That changes the interaction average even when the same orbitals were used.

example.title: A specified pair of orbitals
steps: The one-body sum is 1.40 eV, the direct term 0.30 eV and the exchange term 0.02 eV.
The symmetric spatial average is 1.72 eV; the antisymmetric one is 1.68 eV.

exchange-energy.equation: energy average = one-body sum + direct term ± exchange term

terms.definition: The interaction average from the unswapped product states.
The cross contribution between the direct and swapped products.

lessonCopy.body.1: Expand the interaction expectation in φ_±=(u₁v₂±v₁u₂)/√2. The two direct terms each give J_d; the two cross terms give ±K_ex. For the stated exchange-symmetric real interaction K_ex is real, so ⟨W⟩_±=J_d±K_ex.
lessonCopy.body.2: If the one-body orbital energies are ε_u and ε_v, their sum is the same in these two chosen states. Thus the full energy expectations are ε_u+ε_v+J_d±K_ex. The symmetric spatial state pairs with a spin singlet, and the antisymmetric spatial state with a spin triplet for electrons.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Suppose the specified orbitals give ε_u+ε_v=1.40 eV, J_d=0.30 eV and K_ex=+0.02 eV.
lessonCopy.practice.prompt: Use two orthonormal spatial orbitals with one-body energy sum 0.80 eV, direct integral 0.25 eV and exchange integral +0.03 eV. Separately count two spinless fermions in three orthogonal complete modes.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.feedback: Choose occupied pairs 01,02 or 12; no duplicated complete mode.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.2.description: Star conjugates amplitudes. Orthogonality makes the pair normalization √2 valid.

spin-sequence-capstone.idea: Include every recorded selection when calculating a spin sequence.
spin-sequence-capstone.explanation: A rotation sets amplitudes, then the first selected measurement prepares the input for the next. Multiply the first chance by the next conditional chance; an omitted measurement would describe another experiment.

example.title: A rotation followed by two filters
steps: Rotate +z by π/3 about y. A +z filter then succeeds with probability 3/4.
For that selected state, a −x filter succeeds with probability 1/2. The full success chance is 3/8.

terms.definition: A built-in form of quantum angular momentum with specific possible readings. Even a particle modeled as a point can have spin.

A number used to combine quantum possibilities. For a single normalized reference state, square the size of its amplitude to get the chance of that outcome. For position, this gives a density that you add over a region.

lessonCopy.body.0: Prepare |+z⟩=(1,0)ᵀ and apply an active y rotation U_y(θ)=exp(−iθσ_y/2). The output spinor is (cos(θ/2),sin(θ/2))ᵀ. These are amplitudes; the rotation angle is θ, while the spinor uses half-angles.
lessonCopy.body.1: Next record a successful +z projection and then a successful −x projection. The first probability is cos²(θ/2). Its conditioned state is +z, so the later −x probability is 1/2. The whole sequence has probability (1/2)cos²(θ/2).
lessonCopy.body.2: If there is no intermediate z measurement, the −x probability is instead |[cos(θ/2)−sin(θ/2)]/√2|²=(1−sinθ)/2. The two questions describe different physical procedures, not conflicting predictions.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Take θ=π/3. The rotated state is (√3/2,1/2)ᵀ. The +z selection probability is 3/4.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: The later −x conditional probability is 1/2, giving joint probability 3/8=0.375.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: Without the intermediate z measurement, the −x chance would be (1−√3/2)/2≈0.06699. If z is measured but unread, it is 1/2. These are three different experiments.
lessonCopy.check.prompt: Change θ to 2π/3 but keep the selected +z then −x sequence. What is its joint probability?
lessonCopy.apply.text: Which preparation should be used after a recorded successful +z filter?
lessonCopy.apply.answer: Use |+z⟩, not the earlier rotated superposition. Keeping the old state would ignore the specified conditioning. Conversely, do not apply a measurement update if no measurement actually happened.
lessonCopy.practice.prompt: Prepare +z, rotate by θ=π/2 about y, then compare the three procedures described in the lesson.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.0.label: Probability of the first +z filter
lessonCopy.practice.parts.1.label: Joint probability of selected +z then −x
lessonCopy.practice.parts.2.feedback: The rotated state is +x, orthogonal to −x.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.feedback: Average 1/2 over the two z branches.
lessonCopy.equationGuide.symbols.1.description: Their physical component outcomes are ±ℏ/2. In z coordinates,|−x⟩=(1,−1)ᵀ/√2.

two-level-capstone.idea: The largest transfer a drive can cause and the transfer at this instant are different numbers.
two-level-capstone.explanation: A mismatch between the drive and the gap between the two levels can limit how much chance moves to the second state. The drive duration tells where the back-and-forth transfer has reached. Include both effects before predicting the reading.

example.title: A detuned constant Hamiltonian
steps: Use detuning energy 6 eV and coupling 4 eV. The splitting size d is √(3² + 4²) = 5 eV.
At dt/ℏ = π/2, transfer reaches 16/25, or 64%.

terms.definition: Coupling energy.
Half the energy gap, √[(Δ/2)² + g²].
Detuning energy.
Elapsed time.
Planck’s constant divided by 2π.
Chance of finding reference state one after starting in zero.

lessonCopy.body.0: Use the time-independent Hamiltonian H=(Δ/2)σ_z+gσ_x in the ordered reference basis (|0⟩,|1⟩). Both Δ and the real coupling g are energies. Let d=√[(Δ/2)²+g²], so H²=d²I and the two energy eigenvalues are ±d.
lessonCopy.body.1: The exact evolution is U=cos(dt/ℏ)I−i sin(dt/ℏ)H/d for d>0. Starting in |0⟩ gives the transition probability P₁(t)=(g²/d²)sin²(dt/ℏ). A nonzero detuning reduces its maximum; changing the time phase controls where the oscillation is within that bound.
lessonCopy.body.2: The initial energy expectation is Δ/2, and its energy-eigenstate probabilities are [1±Δ/(2d)]/2. Those weights remain constant under this H even though the reference-basis populations change. Off-diagonal coherence contributes to the energy expectation in the reference basis.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Choose Δ=6 eV and g=4 eV. Then d=5 eV, the energy eigenvalues are ±5 eV, and the maximum reference-state transfer is 16/25=0.64.
lessonCopy.example.steps.1: At dt/ℏ=π/2, the state is (−0.6i,−0.8i)ᵀ and has norm one. Its |1⟩ probability is 0.64.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: The energy probabilities remain 0.8 for +5 eV and 0.2 for −5 eV, with mean 3 eV. Calculating only the diagonal population contribution would miss the off-diagonal coherence term needed for that conserved mean.
lessonCopy.check.explanations.2: Detuning limits the maximum to 0.64 in this model.
lessonCopy.practice.prompt: Change to Δ=8 eV and g=3 eV, starting in |0⟩, and consider dt/ℏ=π/2.
lessonCopy.practice.parts.3.feedback: The initial |0⟩ expectation is Δ/2=4 eV.

composite-exchange-capstone.idea: Knowing a pair’s entire wave still need not give a separate wave for either partner.
composite-exchange-capstone.explanation: A pure pair can contain information about which readings occur together. To predict one partner’s results alone, add over all readings of the other. Its table can describe a mixture even though the complete pair has a single wave description.

example.title: A weighted entangled pair
steps: Prepare √(3/4)|00⟩ + i√(1/4)|11⟩. The first partner has probabilities 3/4 and 1/4.
Its local purity is (3/4)² + (1/4)² = 5/8, although the full pair is pure.

terms.definition: The first partner’s reduced density matrix.
The sum of diagonal entries.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.

lessonCopy.body.0: First consider two distinguishable spin-one-half systems A and B in ψ=√(3/4)|00⟩+i√(1/4)|11⟩. Tracing out B gives ρ_A=diag(3/4,1/4). Its purity is Tr(ρ_A²)=5/8, even though the joint state is pure.
lessonCopy.body.1: If B is measured in the plus/minus basis and the + result is recorded, that result has probability 1/2. The conditioned A state is √(3/4)|0⟩+i√(1/4)|1⟩, a pure state. If B’s result is ignored, averaging both branches restores the same ρ_A as before. Conditioning and unconditioned local statistics answer different questions.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: The joint coefficient weights are 3/4 and 1/4. The local purity is (3/4)²+(1/4)²=10/16=5/8.

quantum2-assessment.idea: Before using a table of numbers as a quantum state, check that it gives sensible probabilities.
quantum2-assessment.explanation: This table is called a density matrix. Its diagonal numbers must add to one. Opposite entries must match after reversing the sign of their imaginary parts. Its eigenvalues, the weights on its independent states, must all be zero or positive. Entries away from the diagonal can also affect the result of a measurement.

example.title: A mixed-state plus-y test
steps: Use ρ = [[0.6,0.2i],[−0.2i,0.4]], which passes the state checks.
The +y probability is 0.30. Using only the diagonal weights would incorrectly give 0.50.

terms.definition: The density matrix.
The selected outcome’s projector.
Add the diagonal entries after multiplying.
The imaginary unit, with i² = −1.
A table used to predict quantum measurement results. It can describe one prepared state or a random mixture of preparations.
The number that a matrix or other linear rule multiplies a matching eigenvector by.

lessonCopy.body.0: For a finite density operator, first check ρ†=ρ, Trρ=1 and nonnegative eigenvalues. Trace one alone is not enough. The probability of a projective outcome P is Tr(ρP), and the expectation of an observable A is Tr(ρA). Their units differ if A is dimensional.
lessonCopy.example.steps.0: Use ρ=[[0.6,0.2i],[−0.2i,0.4]]. It is Hermitian with trace one and eigenvalues (1±√0.2)/2, both positive.
lessonCopy.example.steps.2: For the +y projector onto (1,i)ᵀ/√2, the probability is 0.30. The imaginary off-diagonal entries matter; keeping only the diagonal weights would incorrectly give 1/2.
lessonCopy.check.prompt: Is ρ=[[0.5,0.8],[0.8,0.5]] a valid density matrix?
